newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE-"Ragtime, "Jane Eyre" preen with eyes on Broadway.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-"Ragtime, "Jane Eyre" preen with eyes on Broadway.

text.p: While Broadway waits to see whether a musical based on the Titanic disaster will sink without a trace when it opens next year, Toronto has been busy coming up with musicals on subjects almost as unlikely.

The announced date for the opening of "Titanic" on Broadway is April and it has spurred a newspaper debate on musicals with unlikely subjects -- with the conclusion that if a show is good, anything goes.

Meanwhile, musical productions of Charlotte Bronte's novel "Jane Eyre" and E.L. Doctorow's "Ragtime" are competing for audiences in Canada's largest city in preparation for Broadway next year. Both have had their complex plots condensed, especially Doctorow's epic novel of early 20th century America, and have given over their emotional voices to musical scores in order to take on stage identities.

Bronte's 19th century "tale of spiritual growth and love" seems odd fodder for a musical but its backers hope it will attract the same audiences who have been filling movie houses across North America for film versions of Jane Austin's novels "Sense and Sensibility" and "Emma."

Privately owned Mirvish Productions is betting $4.4 million that its "Jane Eyre" production, which opened in November at Toronto's Royal Alexandra theatre, will take Broadway by storm in the spring or autumn of 1997.

"Ragtime" depicts the rich, the oppressed and the newly arrived in a gilded age. It blends the lives of common folk and fictional characters with such historical figures as financier J.P. Morgan, anarchist Emma Goldman and famed escape artist Harry Houdini.

The $8 million production was developed by veteran stage and entertainment company Livent Inc. The musical version, which made its world premiere in Toronto on Dec. 8, is expected on Broadway by late 1997.

Livent's Broadway productions have collectively won 12 Tony awards including best musical for "Kiss of the Spider Woman" and best musical revival for "Show Boat," which is expected to have earned $100 million by January 1997.

"Jane Eyre" is the first large-scale production with which Mirvish has been involved from the start. It usually buys into existing plays such as "Beauty and the Beast," "Les Miserables" and "Miss Saigon" for its two theatres in Toronto.

The stage show of "Ragtime," which Variety called "robust at best, bombastic at worst," is an edited version of Doctorow's complex novel, with a reduced plotline and stock characters to fit his rich text into a musical production.

Doctorow's graceful 1975 book is a skilful mosaic of fact, fiction and numerous storylines woven together with supreme artistry; the novel's haunting effect is produced as much by what is left unwritten as by what is written.
"Such subtlety is not typically the province of big-budget musicals," the Variety reviewer wrote.
JANE EYRE MUSICAL FAITHFUL TO BOOK
Even the most ardent purists will concede that "Jane Eyre" is entirely faithful to the spirit and language of Bronte's work, published in 1847 and an instant literary success.

Despite the large amount of internal dialogue and the complex themes of Bronte's novel, director John Caird believed "Jane Eyre" would translate successfully into a musical. "The addition of powerful emotional music can far more successfully transform something from the literary form to the dramatic form," Caird told Reuters.

But many of the same difficulties apparent in "Ragtime" are also present for "Jane Eyre," which compresses much of the early action of the novel into an almost frenetic montage to fit the story into a stage production format. The childhood of Jane Eyre, a stoic governess with more inner fire than outer beauty, is suggested with swift brush strokes.

But Caird believes the production will be accepted by Broadway audiences looking for new concepts. "I think it should be very successful in New York," he said. "There's a sense these days that maybe we've gone a bit too far down the road in musicals where the sets do most of the dancing and money does most of the talking."
